client: I've been really anxious about something coming up this weekend — my partner wants me to meet their friends for the first time, and I can't stop dreading it. I keep imagining them judging me or thinking I'm not good enough for my partner, and it's been keeping me up at night. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to make the anxiety go away, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when you're not sure it'll help, and I'm really glad you did. What you're describing — that loop of imagining judgment and feeling like you might not measure up — sounds exhausting, especially when it's stealing your sleep. I'm curious: when you picture these friends forming that negative opinion of you, what's the very first thought that tends to pop into your mind?

client: Honestly, the first thought that pops up is something like "they're going to realize I'm not as interesting or capable as they thought I was." It's like I'm waiting for the moment they finally see through me and decide I'm not worth their time. And the worst part is I can't even point to anything specific they've done to make me feel that way — it just feels like this constant background hum that I can't turn off.
therapist: What you're describing — that sense of waiting to be "found out" — is something many people experience, and it has a name: impostor feelings, and they can feel incredibly real even without any concrete evidence to support them. It's actually really significant that you noticed there's nothing specific these friends have done to trigger this; that kind of self-awareness is a powerful first step in gently questioning whether that thought is a fact or a fear your mind is treating *as* a fact. If a close friend came to you with this same worry before meeting new people, what evidence do you think you'd help them look for to test whether that thought was actually true?

client: I mean, I guess if a friend said that to me, I'd probably tell them to think about times people actually seemed to enjoy their company or wanted to hang out again. But it feels different when it's me — like, I can list those things in my head and still have this voice that says "yeah, but they just don't know the real you yet." It's like the evidence doesn't stick the same way it would for someone else.
therapist: You've just spotted something really important — you already *have* the tools to challenge this thought, but there's a part of your mind that moves the goalposts the moment you try to use them, which is such a common but frustrating feature of anxiety. That "yeah, but they don't know the real you" voice is worth getting curious about: it's essentially claiming there's a hidden "real you" that's somehow worse than the person your friends and partner actually experience — and I wonder if that version even exists, or if it's more like a story anxiety is telling you. What do you think the people who *do* know you well — your partner, close friends — would say if you asked them to describe the "real you"?

client: I think they'd probably say nice things, yeah, but that almost makes it worse in a way — like, what if they're just being kind because they love me and don't want to hurt me? It's hard to trust the positive feedback when there's this nagging feeling that if they really saw everything, all my doubts and the times I've been selfish or snapped at someone, they'd think differently. I know that sounds like I'm just rejecting every piece of evidence that contradicts the anxiety, but I genuinely can't tell if I'm being realistic or if the anxiety is just winning again.
therapist: The fact that you can step back and ask "am I being realistic, or is anxiety winning?" shows real insight — that's not a small thing. What you're describing is a kind of moving target where positive evidence gets disqualified as bias, which means the anxiety has set up a game it can never lose — and that's worth noticing, because no amount of evidence will ever feel like "enough" when the rules are rigged that way. I'm wondering: do you think your partner's friends, or anyone really, would need you to be completely free of doubts, selfishness, or hard moments to be worth knowing — or is that a standard you'd apply to anyone else you care about?

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. Like, no, I wouldn't expect my friends to be perfect or doubt-free before I decided they were worth knowing. But it feels different when it's me, because I'm the one who knows all my flaws from the inside, and I guess I worry that if they really saw all of that, they'd feel the same way I do about myself.
therapist: You've just uncovered something really tender and important there — the harshest critic in the room isn't these friends you haven't even met yet, it's you, and you're essentially worried they'll eventually agree with a judgment you've already made about yourself. That gap between how you'd treat a friend versus how you treat yourself is worth sitting with, because it suggests the core issue might be less about what these new people will think and more about what you think of you. What do you imagine it might feel like to meet these friends this weekend if you tried, even just as an experiment, to extend yourself the same basic generosity you'd offer a friend in your shoes?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right, but honestly it feels almost impossible to imagine being that kind to myself in the moment. Like, when I'm actually standing there at that gathering, trying to make conversation, the self-critical voice just gets so loud that I don't know how I'd even remember to be gentle with myself. I guess I'm also a little scared that if I try this "experiment" and it still goes badly, it'll just confirm everything I already believe about myself.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — it feels like trying the experiment raises the stakes, because now there's something to lose if it doesn't go perfectly. But I want to gently offer a reframe: what if "going badly" and "confirming your worst fears" aren't actually the same thing — like, even an awkward conversation or a quiet moment doesn't really prove you're unworthy, it just proves you're human in a room full of other humans who've also had awkward moments. What would it look like to define success this weekend not as "they loved me" but as something smaller and more in your control — like simply showing up and being present?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically, but it's hard to really believe it in the moment when I'm actually there. Like, I can tell myself "awkward is just human" all I want, but when people go quiet or change the subject after I say something, my brain immediately jumps to "see, they don't want you here." I guess I'm worried that redefining success as just "showing up" feels like setting the bar so low that I'm basically already admitting I'll fail at the real thing.
therapist: It's really worth noticing that your mind just framed "showing up with kindness toward yourself" as failure — which tells us how high and unmovable the bar anxiety has set actually is, because even self-compassion gets recast as defeat. Those quiet moments or subject changes you mentioned are real, but they're also genuinely ambiguous — there are so many reasons a conversation shifts that have nothing to do with you, and your brain is currently trained to pick the most painful explanation by default. I'm curious: after this weekend, what's one small thing you could pay attention to — maybe a moment of genuine laughter, or someone asking you a follow-up question — that you'd be willing to hold onto as real data, even if the anxious voice tries to explain it away?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I know logically that conversations shift for all kinds of reasons, but in the moment it just feels so obvious that it's me, you know? Like my brain doesn't even pause to consider other explanations, it just goes straight to "they're bored of you." And the idea of holding onto a positive moment as "real data" sounds nice, but I'm already kind of dreading that my anxiety will just immediately find a way to dismiss whatever I notice, like "oh they only laughed because they felt sorry for you" or something like that.
therapist: You're essentially describing your anxiety as a defense attorney that can discredit any witness — and you're right that it's very good at that job, which is exactly why trying to *out-argue* it in the moment rarely works. Instead of trying to collect evidence that convinces the anxious voice, what if the small experiment this weekend was just about noticing when your brain makes that instant leap to "it's me," pausing for even two seconds, and asking "what's one other possible explanation" — not to prove the anxiety wrong, but just to slow the automatic jump down a little? Does that feel like something that might be manageable in the moment, even when things feel intense?

client: I mean... I guess that sounds more doable than what I thought you were going to suggest. But honestly, even that two-second pause feels like a lot when I'm already in it — like when my coworker went quiet in the meeting yesterday, my brain had already decided it was my fault before I even consciously registered what was happening. I'm not sure I'll actually remember to pause in those moments, it kind of just takes over.
therapist: What you're describing - the anxiety moving faster than conscious thought - is really real, and it's actually not a personal failing, it's just how deeply practiced that mental habit has become over time, which means it'll take some gentle repetition to slow it down rather than one perfect moment of insight. Rather than catching it *in* the moment this weekend, what if the experiment was even simpler — just noticing it *afterward*, like "huh, my brain did that jump again," without judgment, almost like you're a curious observer of your own mind rather than someone who has to fix it in real time. What do you think it would feel like to give yourself permission to notice the pattern *after* it happens, rather than putting pressure on yourself to intercept it while you're already in the thick of it?

client: Honestly, that does sound a little more manageable than what I was picturing, like I was supposed to catch myself mid-spiral and just... stop it somehow. But I'm a little skeptical, because even afterward I tend to just feel embarrassed or frustrated that I went there again, so I'm not sure "curious observer" is a mode I naturally have access to. It feels like the judgment is kind of baked into the noticing, if that makes sense.
therapist: That makes complete sense, and it's a really honest and perceptive thing to notice — for a lot of people, self-awareness and self-criticism have become so tangled together that noticing a pattern and judging yourself for it happen in the same breath. What you're describing is actually the next layer of the work: not just catching the anxious thought, but also catching the "ugh, I did it again" that follows, because that second hit is its own kind of automatic pile-on. I'm wondering — when you imagine a "curious observer" who isn't judgmental, does any person in your life come to mind who embodies that quality, someone whose voice you might be able to borrow, even briefly, when the self-criticism kicks in after the fact?
